promise: After this you can explain how a batch job differs from a stream job, why event time and watermarks matter, and why teams run the same job over history to fix mistakes.

terms.definition: A record that something happened, such as "order 42 was placed", usually with a time on it.
An ordered record of events that readers can read from any position.
A program that reads data, transforms it and writes a result.

stages.name: Basics
body: A batch job runs over data that is all there before it starts, and ends when it has processed it. A streaming job is meant to stay online indefinitely and process data as it arrives. Flink calls the first kind of input bounded, because all of it is known before the job runs, and the second unbounded [[flink-exec]].

Flink and Beam both treat these as two settings of one model, not two products. Flink runs the same DataStream program in either mode over bounded input, and says the final results are the same, though a streaming run may emit incremental updates on the way [[flink-exec]]. Beam describes itself as a unified model for batch and streaming pipelines [[beam-basics]].

terms.definition: Input whose full content is known before the job runs [[flink-exec]].
Input that keeps arriving, potentially indefinitely [[flink-exec]].
In Beam, a graph of the reads, transforms and writes in a data processing task [[beam-basics]].

stages.name: How it works
body: Streaming jobs deal with three kinds of time: when an event happened (event time), when the system first saw it (ingestion time) and when an operator processes it (processing time). Event time gives reproducible results because they do not depend on when the job runs [[flink-analytics]].

Events arrive out of order, so a stream job cannot know when a stretch of time is complete. A watermark at time t is a claim that the stream is probably complete up to t, so results for earlier times can be released. Waiting less gives faster, riskier answers; waiting more gives fuller ones later [[flink-analytics]]. An event that turns up after a watermark covering its time counts as late [[flink-analytics]].

In batch mode the input is known in advance, so Flink can treat it as having perfect watermarks, sort by timestamp, and run in stages; it ignores the configured state backend and processes one key at a time [[flink-exec]].

terms.definition: The time an event occurred, recorded by the device producing it [[flink-analytics]].
An assertion that the stream is probably complete up to a time [[flink-analytics]].
An event whose timestamp is at or before a watermark that came earlier [[flink-analytics]].

stages.name: Going deeper
body: To total an unbounded stream you cut it into windows. Flink offers tumbling, sliding and session windows, in event-time and processing-time versions. Processing-time windows are quicker, but they give different results on each run and mishandle old or out-of-order data [[flink-analytics]].

The Dataflow paper from Google frames the work as four questions: what results are computed, where in event time, when in processing time they are materialized, and how earlier results relate to later refinements. It argues that the choice of batch, micro-batch or streaming engine should come down to correctness, latency and cost [[dataflow-paper]]. It also says Lambda systems can meet many requirements but lose on simplicity, because two systems have to be built and maintained [[dataflow-paper]].

Batch mode changes behaviour in ways to know: rolling operations such as reduce() or sum() emit only the final result, and checkpointing does not work, so a transactional sink must use the Unified Sink API [[flink-exec]].

terms.definition: A finite slice of a growing collection, used to group elements by their timestamps [[beam-basics]].
In Beam, what decides when to aggregate the results of each window [[beam-basics]].
A design with separate batch and streaming systems; the paper says it fails on simplicity because two systems must be built and maintained [[dataflow-paper]].

stages.name: In practice and trade-offs
body: Flink's guidance is to use batch mode when the job is bounded because it is more efficient, and streaming mode when it is unbounded. It names bootstrapping state for an unbounded job from a bounded run as a special case, and recommends setting the mode on the command line rather than in the code so the same application runs in either [[flink-exec]].

This is the idea behind the posts on the topic page: keep the streaming job and change where it reads from. How much code changes depends on the application, and the posts show that order and lateness are the hard part, not the source swap.

Running Flink locally is a good way to see the Web UI and what a cluster consists of. The installation page asks for Java 11, 17 or 21 and shows one TaskManager with task slots in the dashboard [[flink-install]].

terms.definition: In Flink's DataStream API, STREAMING (the default), BATCH or AUTOMATIC, set with execution.runtime-mode [[flink-exec]].
Recomputing results over past data. The term is used by the posts; the docs here cover the modes that make it possible.

misconceptions.myth: Batch and streaming need two different programming models.
misconceptions.truth: Flink and Beam both present one model. Flink says a DataStream program over bounded input gives the same final results in either mode [[flink-exec]], and Beam calls itself a unified model for both [[beam-basics]].

misconceptions.myth: A watermark is a guarantee that no more old events will arrive.
misconceptions.truth: It is an assertion that the stream is probably complete up to a time, so an event after it can still be late [[flink-analytics]]. Beam calls it a guess [[beam-basics]].

misconceptions.myth: Batch mode is streaming mode run faster.
misconceptions.truth: Batch mode runs in stages, ignores the state backend, fires all timers at the end of the input and does not support checkpointing [[flink-exec]].
